cards.front: Asexual reproduction has {{c1::one parent}} and makes offspring that are usually genetically the same.
cards.quote: Asexual reproduction has one parent and makes offspring genetically the same, like the runner.
cards.section: One parent or two sex cells

cards.front: Name three examples of asexual reproduction in living things.
cards.back: A potato grows from its eyes, a spider plant makes plantlets, and yeast forms a bud that breaks off.
cards.quote: a potato grows from its eyes, a spider plant makes plantlets, and yeast forms a bud that breaks off.
cards.section: One parent or two sex cells

cards.front: {{c1::Sex cells}} are the cells that carry genetic information to the next generation.
cards.back: In animals, special cells in the ovaries and testes make them.
cards.quote: Sex cells are the cells that carry genetic information to the next generation.
cards.section: One parent or two sex cells

cards.front: A chromosome pair is two chromosomes with the same kinds of genes in the same general places, one from the {{c1::mother}} and one from the father.
cards.quote: A chromosome pair is two chromosomes with the same kinds of genes in the same general places, one from the mother and one from the father.
cards.section: Halve, then restore: the human numbers

cards.front: An {{c1::allele}} is one version of a gene.
cards.back: You carry two alleles of most genes, one on each chromosome of a pair.
cards.quote: An allele is one version of a gene.
cards.section: Count the mixes

cards.front: {{c1::Fertilization}} joins a sperm and an egg into one cell with full pairs again.
cards.quote: Fertilization joins a sperm and an egg into one cell with full pairs again.
cards.section: Halve, then restore: the human numbers

cards.front: In living things with paired chromosomes, what does meiosis do to the chromosome number, and what restores it?
cards.back: Meiosis halves the number, so each sex cell has one chromosome from each pair. Fertilization restores the pairs.
cards.quote: meiosis halves chromosome number and makes mixes; fertilization restores pairs.

cards.front: A typical human body cell has 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs. How many does an egg have, and how many does a fertilized egg have?
cards.back: The egg has 23. The fertilized egg has 46, because 23 (egg) + 23 (sperm) = 46.
cards.quote: A typical human body cell has 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs, so an egg or sperm normally has 23:
cards.section: Halve, then restore: the human numbers

cards.front: Before meiosis, a chromosome is copied. Does the copied chromosome count as two chromosomes? Why or why not?
cards.back: No. A copied chromosome still counts as one chromosome, made of two joined copies.
cards.quote: A copied chromosome still counts as one chromosome, made of two joined copies.
cards.section: Halve, then restore: the human numbers

cards.front: A parent has alleles B and b for one gene. Why does each sex cell have a 50 percent chance of carrying B?
cards.back: The two chromosomes of a pair separate, and each sex cell gets only one of them. B and b each have an equal chance.
cards.quote: You carry two alleles of most genes, one on each chromosome of a pair.
cards.section: Count the mixes

cards.front: In the sorting model, how does one chromosome pair sort compared with the other pairs?
cards.back: Each pair sorts by chance, independently of the other pairs.
cards.quote: each chromosome pair sorts by chance, independently of the other pairs in this model.
cards.section: Count the mixes

cards.front: Compare mitosis and meiosis: what does each make, and how do the new cells compare with the parent cell?
cards.back: Mitosis makes body cells that match the parent cell, for growth and repair. Meiosis makes sex cells with half the chromosomes, which can carry different mixes.
cards.quote: Meiosis halves chromosome number and makes mixes; fertilization restores pairs.
cards.section: Evaluate: check your thinking

cards.front: Why do a strawberry runner and its parent match genetically, while brothers and sisters usually differ?
cards.back: A runner is asexual: one parent usually passes on the same genetic information. Siblings grow from different sex cells made by meiosis, which carry different mixes.
cards.quote: So siblings receive different mixes, while a strawberry runner usually carries its one parent's genetic information.
cards.section: Evaluate: check your thinking

cards.front: In the sorting model, a parent has 3 chromosome pairs that all differ, giving 8 kinds of sex cells. What does a fourth pair do to the number of kinds, and why?
cards.back: It doubles the number to 16. Each pair gives 2 choices, and because the pairs sort independently, the counts multiply: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2.
cards.quote: Because the pairs sort independently, the counts multiply.
cards.section: Count the mixes

cards.front: A fruit fly body cell has 8 chromosomes. In the sorting model, how many pairs is that, and how many kinds of sex cells can it make if every pair differs?
cards.back: 8 chromosomes make 4 pairs. Each pair gives 2 choices, so 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 kinds of whole-chromosome mixes.
cards.quote: Two pairs give 2 × 2 = 4. Three give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.
cards.section: Count the mixes

cards.front: A domestic cat sex cell has 19 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in a cat body cell, and why?
cards.back: 38. A sex cell has half the body-cell number, so the body cell has twice 19.
cards.quote: Body-cell numbers come from published counts. The sex-cell column was calculated by halving, not counted.
cards.section: Evidence: chromosome numbers across living things

cards.front: Find the mean body-cell chromosome number of the four living things with the fewest chromosomes: fruit fly 8, garden pea 14, rice 24, cat 38.
cards.quote: Find the mean body-cell number of the four living things with the fewest chromosomes.
cards.section: Evidence: chromosome numbers across living things

cards.front: A class makes 400 sex cells from a parent with alleles B and b in the sorting model and gets 188 with B and 212 with b. Does this fit the 50 percent rule?
cards.back: Yes. Both counts are close to 200, half of 400. Chance does not promise exact halves.
cards.quote: each sex cell has a 50 percent chance of carrying B and a 50 percent chance of carrying b.
cards.section: Count the mixes

cards.front: Does a bigger chromosome number mean a more complex living thing? Use the chicken (78), human (46) and garden strawberry (56).
cards.back: No. The chicken has more chromosomes than a human, and the strawberry has more than a human. Number alone does not show complexity.
cards.quote: Predict: Does a bigger chromosome number mean a more complex living thing? Compare the chicken and the human, then two more rows.
cards.section: Evidence: chromosome numbers across living things

cards.front: Strawberry plants grown from runners of one parent have leaf lengths with a range of 20 mm. Plants grown from seeds have a range of 45 mm. What does this fit, and what other difference could matter?
cards.back: It fits the idea that asexual offspring share the parent's genetic information, so they vary less. Runner plants may also start with food from the parent, another difference between the groups.
cards.quote: Runner plants may start with food from the parent, another difference between the groups.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: The table of chromosome numbers lists sex-cell numbers that were calculated by halving. Does it test the halving rule? What would?
cards.back: No. It shows the rule but does not test it. A test needs counts from real sex cells.
cards.quote: The calculated column shows the halving rule but does not test it. A test needs counts from real sex cells.
cards.section: Evidence: chromosome numbers across living things

cards.front: Suppose fruit flies, with 8 chromosomes in a body cell, made sex cells that kept all 8 instead of halving. What would a fertilized egg have, and what would happen over generations?
cards.back: A fertilized egg would have 16 chromosomes, then 32 in the next generation, doubling each time. Meiosis halving to 4 per sex cell keeps the number at 8.
cards.quote: Meiosis halves chromosome number and makes mixes; fertilization restores pairs.
